content: Ciprofloxacin Medication Guide CIPRO® (Sip-row) CIPRO® Tablets (ciprofloxacin hydrochloride) CIPRO® Oral Suspension (ciprofloxacin) CIPRO® XR (ciprofloxacin extended-release tablets) CIPRO® IV (ciprofloxacin for intravenous infusion) Before starting CIPRO® and each time you get a refill, read the accompanying Medication Guide carefully. It may contain updated information. This guide is not a substitute for discussing your medical condition or treatment with your healthcare provider. What is the most important information I should know about CIPRO? CIPRO belongs to a class of antibiotics called fluoroquinolones. It can cause serious side effects, some of which may be life-threatening. If you experience any of the following severe side effects, seek medical attention immediately and discuss with your healthcare provider whether you should continue taking CIPRO. 1. Tendon Rupture or Tendon Swelling (Tendinitis): Tendon problems can occur in people of all ages taking CIPRO. Tendons are the tough cords of tissue that connect muscles to bones. Symptoms of tendon issues include pain, swelling, tears, or inflammation in tendons, particularly in the Achilles tendon (back of the ankle), shoulder, hand, or other areas. The risk of tendon problems is higher if you: Are over 60 years old. Are taking corticosteroids (steroids). Have had a kidney, heart, or lung transplant. Tendon problems can also occur in people without these risk factors. Other factors that may increase your risk include physical activity, kidney failure, or a history of tendon issues (e.g., in people with rheumatoid arthritis). At the first sign of tendon pain, swelling, or inflammation, stop taking CIPRO and contact your healthcare provider. Avoid exercise and using the affected area until tendinitis or tendon rupture is ruled out. Tendon rupture can occur during or after completing CIPRO treatment, sometimes even months later. Signs of tendon rupture include: Hearing or feeling a snap or pop in a tendon area. Bruising immediately after an injury in a tendon area. Inability to move the affected area or bear weight. 2. Worsening of Myasthenia Gravis: CIPRO and other fluoroquinolones may worsen symptoms of myasthenia gravis, a condition that causes muscle weakness. Symptoms may include increased muscle weakness or breathing difficulties. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience worsening symptoms. What is CIPRO? CIPRO is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections. It is not effective against viral infections (e.g., colds or flu). Children under 18 years old are at higher risk of musculoskeletal problems (e.g., joint pain or swelling) while taking CIPRO. CIPRO should not be the first choice of antibiotic for children under 18 unless treating specific serious infections, such as complicated urinary tract infections or preventing anthrax after exposure. The safety and effectiveness of CIPRO XR in children under 18 are not established. Who should not take CIPRO? Do not take CIPRO if you: Have had a severe allergic reaction to fluoroquinolone antibiotics or any of the ingredients in CIPRO. Are taking tizanidine (Zanaflex®), as serious side effects may occur. What should I tell my healthcare provider before taking CIPRO? Inform your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions, including if you: Have tendon problems. Have myasthenia gravis. Have central nervous system (CNS) disorders (e.g., epilepsy). Have nerve problems. Have a history of seizures. Have kidney problems (you may need a lower dose). Have rheumatoid arthritis or other joint issues. Have difficulty swallowing pills. Are pregnant or planning to become pregnant (it is unknown if CIPRO harms an unborn child). Are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed (CIPRO passes into breast milk). How should I take CIPRO? Take CIPRO exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. For tablets, take them in the morning and evening at the same time each day. Swallow the tablet whole without splitting, crushing, or chewing. For oral suspension, shake the bottle well for 15 seconds before each use. For CIPRO XR, take it once daily at the same time each day. Swallow the tablet whole. CIPRO IV is administered via slow intravenous infusion over 60 minutes. CIPRO can be taken with or without food but should not be taken with dairy products or calcium-fortified juices alone. Drink plenty of fluids while taking CIPRO. What should I avoid while taking CIPRO? Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how CIPRO affects you, as it may cause dizziness or lightheadedness. Avoid excessive sunlight or tanning beds, as CIPRO can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight, leading to severe sunburn or blisters. Use sunscreen and protective clothing if you must be in sunlight. What are the possible side effects of CIPRO? CIPRO can cause serious side effects, including: Central Nervous System Effects: Seizures, hallucinations, restlessness, anxiety, confusion, depression, or suicidal thoughts. Severe Allergic Reactions: Hives, difficulty breathing, swelling of the lips or face, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (liver problems). Heart Rhythm Changes (QT Prolongation): Fast or irregular heartbeat, fainting. Intestinal Infection (Pseudomembranous Colitis): Watery or bloody diarrhea, stomach cramps, fever. Peripheral Neuropathy: Pain, burning, tingling, or weakness in the arms, hands, legs, or feet. Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia): Especially when taken with certain diabetes medications. Common side effects include nausea, diarrhea, liver function changes, vomiting, rash, vaginal yeast infections, abdominal pain, and headache. How should I store CIPRO? Store CIPRO tablets and oral suspension below 86°F (30°C). Do not freeze the oral suspension, and discard any unused suspension after 14 days. Store CIPRO XR between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep all medications out of reach of children. General Information Do not use CIPRO for conditions it was not prescribed for, and do not share it with others. For more information, consult your healthcare provider or pharmacist.
